summary: A monthly report of ARPANET traffic for December 1973. It tabulates, for each Host, how many packets it sent, split between traffic that stayed within its own node and traffic sent to other nodes, with daily averages. It is a data memo and defines no protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: It is like a monthly count of how many cars used each road, written down so people can see which roads are busy.

questions: how much traffic did the arpanet carry in december 1973
which arpanet hosts were busiest in 1973
subtitle: ARPANET host traffic statistics for December 1973

tldr.problem: ARPANET operators needed a way to understand how the network was actually being used, how much traffic different hosts generated, and how traffic distributed between local and remote nodes.
tldr.mechanism: The Network Control Center compiled monthly traffic statistics, counting outgoing packets at each host and categorizing them as either intra-node (local) or inter-node (network) traffic, then computing daily averages.
tldr.outcome: Network operators gained visibility into usage patterns, which helped them identify busy nodes, plan capacity upgrades, and understand the emerging structure of network communication.

today: RFC 612 is a historical traffic report from the ARPANET's early operations. It documents the network's growth pattern and usage in December 1973 and serves as a baseline for comparison with modern network traffic. The practice of collecting and publishing network statistics continues today, though with vastly larger scales and more sophisticated metrics.

sections.title: The ARPANET Traffic Report
sections.content:
RFC 612 is not a specification or protocol definition—it is a data memo from the ARPANET's Network Control Center documenting actual network usage during December 1973. It tabulates traffic generated by each host on the network, measuring the number of packets each host sent during the month.

The ARPANET by this time included hosts at major institutions: UCLA, SRI (Stanford Research Institute), UCSB, University of Utah, BBN (Bolt, Beranek and Newman), MIT, Harvard, Stanford, UC Berkeley (Ames), Xerox, MITRE, Carnegie Mellon, and many others. The report shows traffic from more than 40 network nodes, providing a comprehensive snapshot of network usage.
sections.plainLanguage: This paper is a monthly report card for the network. It shows how much traffic each computer sent during December 1973.

sections.title: What the Statistics Reveal
sections.content:
The report categorizes each host's traffic into two types: inter-node traffic (packets sent to other network nodes) and intra-node traffic (packets staying within the local node). This distinction reveals how much of the network was being used for wide-area communication versus local computation and file transfer.

The busiest host in December 1973 was ISI Host 1, which generated 10.9 million packets, with 10.4 million inter-node and 538 thousand intra-node. In comparison, many nodes generated much lighter traffic. For example, BELV Host 0 generated only 1,631 packets total for the entire month. The report shows daily averages, revealing that even high-traffic nodes were only using a fraction of the network's capacity.

The overall network statistics show 73.8 million inter-node packets and 16.5 million intra-node packets for December. On average, the network handled about 2.4 million inter-node packets per day, and the average traffic per node-day was about 52,900 inter-node packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Some computers sent a lot of traffic to other computers on the network (inter-node). Some mostly talked to computers right next to them (intra-node). The report shows which computers were busy and which were quiet.

sections.title: Why These Statistics Mattered
sections.content:
Monthly traffic reports were essential for managing the emerging ARPANET. They allowed the Network Control Center and system administrators to identify which nodes were bottlenecks, anticipate when capacity upgrades would be needed, and understand what applications were driving the most network traffic.

The low overall bandwidth usage in December 1973 (measured in packets, not bits, and dominated by local activity) reflects how early the ARPANET was in its development. The network had nowhere near the saturation it would eventually reach. These statistics provided early data about network growth and usage patterns that would inform infrastructure planning in the years to come.

Updates to RFC 612 continued monthly for several years, tracking the growth and evolution of ARPANET traffic through the 1970s. They constitute a valuable historical record of early network usage.
sections.plainLanguage: These numbers help the network managers understand what is happening. Is one computer sending way too much? Is a path getting crowded? Do we need to build bigger pipes? The monthly reports answer these questions.
